sections.html:
Allentown requires a safety and maintenance inspection before a residential or commercial property is sold. The city's pre-sale inspection page describes a visit that checks the property against the Allentown Property Maintenance Code and the zoning rules.

How the pre-sale inspection runs
StageWhat happens
ApplicationFollow the Pre-Sale Inspection Procedure, then apply online for a Pre-Sale permit
InspectionAn inspector schedules the visit
Passing resultThe property receives a Certificate of Compliance before the sale
Violations foundThe seller fixes them, or the buyer agrees to take the repairs on using the city's Acceptance Form
After settlementThe seller or agent submits a Buyer's Information Report within three days

There is no exception for cash or as-is sales, so plan on the inspection whichever way you sell. Call Building Standards and Safety to learn today's fee and how soon an appointment is available, and only then pick a closing date.

Two paths follow a failed visit. Make the repairs and request a second inspection, or find a buyer who will take the work over. That buyer signs the Acceptance Form, so the agreement sits with the city and not only in the sales contract.

Be candid with buyers about problems you cannot fund before closing. Investors and cash buyers frequently agree to the repairs, and raising it before the inspection date goes better than raising it after a failed visit. Keep the Certificate of Compliance with your settlement papers once you have it.

The code is the Allentown Property Maintenance Code plus the zoning rules, so the visit covers more than the living space. Walk the house and yard first and write down anything that looks unsafe or neglected. Loose stair rails, missing detectors, damaged porches, peeling exterior paint and debris in the yard are the sort of items an inspector can note.

Whoever is at the property should be able to let the inspector in and answer questions. If tenants live there, tell them the date in advance. Zoning matters for houses that were split into units years ago. If your building has more units than zoning permits, learn that now, because it changes who can buy it.

Allentown, the Lehigh County seat, is the Lehigh Valley's biggest city. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 126,044 residents, almost the same as the 125,845 counted in 2020. Only 43.2 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied, which means two-family and multi-unit buildings turn up in many sales next to single houses.

The median value of an owner-occupied home is $206,600, median gross rent is $1,317 and median household income is $55,494. Those medians describe the entire city, and an individual house can sell well above or below them. The Allentown School District covers most addresses, though a small area near Trexler Park falls in the Parkland School District, so check yours.

The age and style of houses shift as you cross town.

  • Center City: Victorian and terraced rowhouses, plus loft apartments in converted mills. Old Allentown and the Old Fairgrounds are historic districts.
  • West Park: mostly Victorian and American Craftsman houses, in a historic district with its own home tour.
  • West End: starts roughly at 15th Street, with tree-lined blocks built mostly in the 1920s through the 1940s.
  • East Side and South Side: single and twin homes from the 1940s to the 1960s, with some older Victorians.
  • The Wards: residential blocks east of Center City from the late 19th and early 20th century boom.

Buyers and inspectors judge a house by its age, so know which era yours belongs to and what usually fails first in it.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or multi-unit building
sections.html:
With owners in under half of occupied homes, Allentown has plenty of two-family and multi-unit buildings, and sales of them draw investors. Those buyers will ask for the leases, the rent history and the pre-sale paperwork, and some will want to see each unit.

Give tenants written notice before showings and keep to the lease terms on access. If you are a landlord selling to an investor, mention the county's contact-information rule for non-owner-occupied property. The new owner has 30 days after purchase to comply.

sections.h2: What to bring to the settlement table
sections.html:
Show up with photo ID, every key, garage openers and appliance manuals. Add the Certificate of Compliance, a signed Acceptance Form if one exists, recent tax bills and a mortgage payoff letter when a loan is open. The title company drafts the deed and the settlement sheet. Go through each line of that sheet before signing and question any charge you cannot explain.

After the deed is signed, the report is due three days later, filed by you or your agent. Mark that date before you leave.

Lehigh County assesses every Allentown parcel. The county's base year is 2013, the date of its last countywide reassessment, with values set at 100 percent of fair market value at that time. New construction and demolition change a parcel's assessment in between. The Assessment Office is in Room 517 of the Government Center at 17 South Seventh Street, Allentown, phone 610-782-3038.

  • Appeal deadline: the Board of Assessment Appeals needs an original signed appeal, with the filing fee, in hand by August 1 each year. Postmarks and faxes do not count as timely.
  • Interim appeals: these run from the date printed on a Change of Assessment Notice.
  • Act 29 of 2026: an owner of non-owner-occupied property must send the county contact information within 30 days of buying. Owner-occupants are exempt, so this falls mostly on landlords and investors buying from you.

You can hire an agent, sell it yourself or accept a cash offer. Working with an agent brings in the most buyers, along with showings and an inspection ordered by the buyer. A cash offer drops the mortgage approval stage, the piece of a closing that usually waits on a lender.

All three still require the city's pre-sale permit, so request it early. If you cannot afford the repairs an inspector lists, ask buyers in writing to accept them through the Acceptance Form.

1. Apply online for the Pre-Sale permit and get the inspection on the calendar.
  2. Fix what you can before the inspector arrives, such as railings, smoke detectors and exterior upkeep.
  3. Collect your deed, your tax bills and any permit records.
  4. Compare offers by what you take home, and ask each buyer how violations will be handled.
  5. Close, then file the Buyer's Information Report within three days.

A cash buyer has no lender appraisal to wait on, so the inspection and the title search decide your closing date.

faqs.q: Do I need an inspection before selling my Allentown house?
faqs.a: Yes. The city requires a pre-sale safety and maintenance inspection for residential and commercial property. A house that passes receives a Certificate of Compliance before the sale.

faqs.q: Can the buyer take over repairs the inspector finds?
faqs.a: Yes. The seller can repair the violations, or the buyer can agree to take them on. That agreement is recorded on the city's Acceptance Form.

faqs.q: What do I file after an Allentown closing?
faqs.a: A Buyer's Information Report goes to the city within three days of settlement. The seller or the real estate agent can submit it.

faqs.q: Which school district serves my Allentown home?
faqs.a: Most of the city is in the Allentown School District, but a small area near Trexler Park is in the Parkland School District. Check your exact address with the district.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Lehigh County assessment?
faqs.a: August 1 each year. The Board of Assessment Appeals needs the original signed appeal and the filing fee by then, and postmarks and faxes are not accepted.
